subject: Cognitive Science
title: The Wug Test
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Wug Test.

hook.text: "This is a wug. Now there are two of them. There are two…" The child says "wugs." She applied the rule.

buildup.text: Jean Berko Gleason's 1958 test proved children extract grammar rules, not just memorized forms.

discovery.text: Kids applied plural (-s), past tense (-ed), and possessive (-'s) to words they'd never heard.

twist.text: Errors like "goed" and "mouses" are signs of progress—they prove the child learned a rule.

climax.text: The wug test is one of the most replicated studies in linguistics. Grammar is rule-based.

punchline.text: Kids don't memorize language. They crack it.

quiz.question: What did the Wug Test demonstrate?
options: Children apply grammar rules to novel words
Children only memorize words they hear
Grammar is taught explicitly by parents

details.summary: Jean Berko Gleason's wug test showed that even young children internalize grammatical rules rather than simply memorizing word forms. When shown a novel creature called a wug and asked about two of them, children correctly say wugs, demonstrating productive use of the plural rule.
details.whyItMatters: The wug test proved that language acquisition involves learning abstract rules, not just copying adults. It was landmark evidence for the creativity of children's grammar.
takeaways: Children apply grammar rules to words they have never heard
The wug test demonstrated productive morphological knowledge
Overregularization errors like goed confirm rule learning

faq.question: What is overregularization and why does it matter?
faq.answer: Overregularization is when children apply a rule too broadly, saying goed instead of went or mouses instead of mice. These errors reveal that children have extracted a rule and are applying it productively. They are actually a sign of linguistic progress, not regression.

faq.question: At what age do children pass the wug test?
faq.answer: Most children demonstrate productive plural use by age four or five. Younger children may struggle with less common morphological patterns. The test has been adapted for many languages and consistently shows that children learn rules, not just individual word forms.
